title: Dedicated capacity demand triage — SLA tiering, GPU classing & scaling runbook
creator: Asha Patel
description: Runbook for evaluating enterprise dedicated capacity requests from intake to commitment. Covers demand signal collection, prioritization rubric, SLA tier definitions, mapping reserved throughput to GPU classes, scalable autoscaling templates, fallback and rollback policy, and handoffs for sales/solutions engineering. Designed to standardize decisions and shorten intake-to-commit timelines for Dedicated and Private deployments.
intake_checklist: Customer basic info: org name, contact, legal entity, region(s)
Workload profile: average qps, peak qps, average tokens per request, percent streaming vs non-streaming
Model and variant: exact model family + pinned version, expected sequence length distribution
SLA targets: p95 latency target, throughput (requests/sec or tokens/sec), availability SLO
Data posture: will data stay in VPC/on-prem? encryption/KMS needs?
Security & compliance: required certifications (SOC2, HIPAA, FedRAMP), network isolation needs
Budget / commitment horizon: monthly commit, annual, burst allowances
Failure tolerance: acceptable degradation modes, fallback models, customer opt-in for graceful degradation
prioritization_rubric: 1) Safety & compliance constraints (regulatory customers with strict isolation) — highest priority
2) Revenue signal: signed or committed ARR / renewal likelihood within quarter
3) Product fit & strategic alignment: new vertical or anchor customer enabling partnerships
4) Technical risk & runway: expected engineering effort (integration, custom networking, audits)
5) Operational complexity: multi-region, burst patterns, special hardware requirements
6) Migration friction: how many existing API changes or model variations required
sla_tiers: Tier C (Bulk): 99.5% availability, best-effort latency — reserved throughput per pool, no guaranteed p95; suitable for non-customer-facing batch workloads
Tier B (Business): 99.9% availability, p95 latency guardrails (e.g., < 500ms for short-generation workloads) — moderate reservation and pre-warmed capacity
Tier A (Enterprise): 99.95% availability, strict p95 latency targets (e.g., <= 250ms for interactive paths), dedicated node pools, cross-region failover and on-call support

Each tier includes burst policy definitions: burst multiplier (x1.5 for B, x2 for A) and max burst window (30s–5min). Bursts are allowed only when pool headroom exists and are chargeable as overage or consumed from committed burst credits.
gpu_mapping: Small (entry reserved): T4 / A10 — low cost, good for non-streaming short-context RAG or embeddings where throughput is modest
Medium (balanced): A30 / RTX5000-class — preferred for mixed workloads (moderate seq lengths, moderate concurrency)
Large (high throughput): A100 40/80GB, H100 — recommended for large seq length generation, high token-per-second needs, or models requiring >30k KV cache
Notes: prefer more medium-class nodes vs single large node for better isolation and parallelism; GPU selection also depends on quantization support and model kernel availability per runtime release
scaling_policy_templates: Steady reserved: maintain N pre-warmed nodes to meet guaranteed reserved throughput. Autoscale only for replacement during failure with manual review for horizontal scale-up.

Demand-aware autoscale (recommended for Tier B): baseline reserved nodes for commit; automatic upscale when sustained >70% CPU/GPU utilization for 60s, downscale after 10m of <30% utilization. Cooldown windows enforced to avoid oscillation.

Aggressive burst autoscale (Tier A burst mode): allow short-lived vertical bursting using pre-allocated burst credit and ephemeral nodes spun from a burst pool. Ephemeral nodes are capped and expire after burst window. All burst instantiation must pass security and KMS policy checks.
Canary rollout policy for capacity changes: apply to 5% of customer traffic in a secondary region for 30 minutes, monitor latency/error budget metrics, roll forward or rollback based on thresholds.
tradeoffs_and_notes: Tradeoff: commit to larger reserved GPUs -> fewer nodes but higher single-node isolation risk vs smaller GPUs -> better failover and packing efficiency
Tradeoff: aggressive autoscaling reduces cost but increases chance of cold starts impacting p95; mitigate with pre-warm heuristics and short-lived caching layers
Note: KV cache sizing must be estimated from expected sequence length distribution and user concurrency. Underprovisioned KV cache leaks directly into latency regressions for stateful chat workloads.
Note: network egress and cross-region routing add non-trivial latency for private deployments; explicitly model egress in capacity calculations.
decisions: Adopt SLA tier definitions (C/B/A) above as default for enterprise intake — approved 2026-03-12 by PM & Infra leads
Default GPU mapping will prioritize A30-class for new medium-sized commitments unless customer requests H100/A100 explicitly — provisional decision pending cost analysis
Require an onboarding checklist sign-off from Solutions Engineering and Security before any Tier A commit is finalized
open_questions: What is the canonical formula to convert customer "requests/sec + avg tokens" into reserved GPU counts for quantized vs fp16 models? (Action: Research to produce conversion table)

Policy: how many bursts and total burst-credit per month should be included per commit tier? Recommended: discuss with finance.
